sections.title: Call and Mission
sections.description: Ezekiel's call vision by the Kebar River, the throne-chariot, and his mission as a prophet

sections.title: Judgment against Jerusalem
sections.description: Sign-acts, visions, and words of judgment against Jerusalem and Judah for their idolatry and unfaithfulness

sections.title: Words of Judgment against the Nations
sections.description: Prophecies against Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre, Sidon, and Egypt

sections.title: Restoration and a New Temple
sections.description: Promises of Israel's restoration, the valley of dry bones, Gog and Magog, and the vision of the new temple

events.title: Ezekiel's call vision by the Kebar River
events.description: In the thirtieth year, while Ezekiel is among the exiles by the Kebar River in Babylon, the heavens open and he sees God's visions. He sees a storm wind from the north with a great cloud and flaming fire, and in its midst four living creatures, each with four faces and four wings. Above their heads rests something like a throne of sapphire, and on the throne a figure with a human appearance surrounded by a radiance like a rainbow. Ezekiel falls on his face, and God's voice calls him to be a prophet for Israel's rebellious people.

events.title: Ezekiel Eats the Scroll
events.description: God reaches out his hand to Ezekiel with a scroll written on both sides with laments, sighs, and woe-cry. God commands him to eat the scroll and then go and speak to the house of Israel. Ezekiel eats the scroll, and it tastes as sweet as honey in his mouth. God sends him to the exiled Israelites, not to foreign peoples with unintelligible speech, but to his own people who still will not listen.

events.title: Ezekiel as Watchman
events.description: God appoints Ezekiel as a watchman for the house of Israel. His task is to warn the wicked when God's word comes to him. If he warns the wicked and they do not turn from their ways, the wicked shall die in their sin, but Ezekiel will have saved his own life. But if Ezekiel fails to warn them, God will require the blood of the wicked at Ezekiel's hand. Ezekiel is also told to shut himself inside his house, and God makes his tongue stick to the roof of his mouth so that he can speak only when God opens his mouth.

events.title: The Sign-Act with the Brick – The Siege of Jerusalem
events.description: God commands Ezekiel to perform a series of symbolic actions that warn of Jerusalem's siege and fall. He is to carve an image of Jerusalem on a brick and lay siege against it. Then he must lie on his left side for 390 days for Israel's sake, and on his right side for 40 days for Judah's sake. He shall eat emergency rations of bread baked over cow dung and drink water in limited amounts. Finally, he is to take a sharp sword and divide his hair into three parts as a sign that one-third of the people will die by plague, one-third by the sword, and one-third will be scattered to all winds.

events.title: The Glory of the Lord Leaves the Temple
events.description: In the sixth year, Ezekiel is taken in a vision to Jerusalem and sees the abominable things that are happening in the temple. He sees images of idols carved into the walls, seventy elders of Israel offering incense to idol statues in dark rooms, women weeping for the god Tammuz, and men worshiping the sun with their backs turned toward the Lord's temple. The glory of God, which had been above the cherubim in the Most Holy Place, lifts up and moves to the threshold of the temple, then to the east gate, and finally leaves the city completely and stands on the mountain east of the city.

events.title: The Sign-Act of Moving
events.description: God commands Ezekiel to pack his belongings in a bag for the journey of exile while the people watch. In the evening he shall dig through the wall and carry his things out into the darkness with his face covered. This act is a sign for the house of Israel: the prince in Jerusalem shall carry his belongings on his shoulder in the darkness, and he shall be caught in Babylon's net and led to the land of Babylon without seeing it. The prophecy points to King Zedekiah's flight and capture, when his eyes were put out before he was taken to Babylon.

events.title: The Parable of the Vine and Jerusalem as an Unfaithful Wife
events.description: God asks Ezekiel what the wood of a vine is better than other trees. It is useless for any work and is thrown into the fire. So it is with the people of Jerusalem: God will hand them over to the fire. In an extended allegory, God tells Jerusalem's story as an abandoned, bloody foundling whom He raised, adorned, and made queen. But Jerusalem became unfaithful and committed adultery with all her neighboring peoples. The city has been worse than Sodom and Samaria, yet God will remember His covenant and establish an everlasting covenant with her.

events.title: Allegory of the Two Sisters Oholah and Oholibamah
events.description: God tells Ezekiel about two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. Both practiced prostitution already in Egypt during their youth. Oholah (Samaria) sought the lovers of Assyria and was finally handed over to them, who killed her with the sword. But Oholibah (Jerusalem) did not learn from her sister’s fate and became even worse in her unfaithfulness. She sought both Assyrian and Babylonian lovers. Therefore God will stir up her lovers against her, and they shall come with armies and weapons to judge her for her unfaithfulness and bloodshed.

events.title: The Death of Ezekiel's Wife
events.description:
God tells Ezekiel to take away his beloved one with a blow, but he must not mourn, weep, or shed tears.  
He is to sigh in silence and hold no funeral lament.  
In the morning Ezekiel proclaims this to the people, and in the evening his wife dies.  
Ezekiel obeys God’s command and does not mourn.  
The people ask what this means, and Ezekiel explains that God will desecrate His temple, their beloved one and pride, and that sons and daughters will fall by the sword.  
On that day Ezekiel’s mouth will be opened, and he will no longer be silent.

events.title: Oracle Against Tyre
events.description: Ezekiel proclaims a series of judgments against the powerful trading city of Tyre, which rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall and saw it as an opportunity for increased wealth. God will raise many nations against Tyre like waves of the sea, and Nebuchadnezzar will besiege the city. The walls and towers of Tyre will be torn down, and stones and soil will be cast into the sea. The prophecy also contains a lament over Tyre as a magnificent ship that sank in the depths of the sea, and a judgment against the king of Tyre who, in his pride, said: I am a god, but he will be cast down to death.

events.title: Oracle Against Egypt
events.description: Ezekiel uttaler a long series of prophecies against Egypt and Pharaoh, who is compared to a great sea monster lying in its Nile arms and saying: "The Nile is mine; I have made it." God will put hooks in the jaws of the monster and drag it out of the water. Egypt shall become a desolate land for forty years, and the people shall be scattered among the nations. The Egyptians shall never again rule over other peoples. Pharaoh is also compared to a mighty cedar on Lebanon that is cut down, and to those who go down to the grave together with all the great nations that have fallen.

events.title: The Fall of Jerusalem Reported
events.description: In the twelfth year of the exile, on the fifth day of the tenth month, a fugitive comes to Ezekiel and reports that Jerusalem has fallen. The evening before, the hand of the Lord had been upon Ezekiel, and when the fugitive arrives in the morning, his mouth is opened and he is no longer mute. God renews Ezekiel’s call as watchman for the house of Israel and warns those remaining in the devastated land not to inherit the land merely because they are few. Those who remain eat blood, worship idols, and shed blood; they shall die by the sword, by wild beasts, and by plague.

events.title: The Good Shepherd
events.description:
God speaks through Ezekiel against Israel's shepherds (leaders) who have only cared for themselves instead of tending the sheep.  
They have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, or sought out the lost, but have ruled over them with harshness.  
Therefore God himself will be shepherd to his sheep.  
He will seek them out, gather them from all the lands where they are scattered, and bring them to good pastures on the mountains of Israel.  
He will raise up one shepherd over them, his servant David, who will tend them and be their prince forever.

events.title: The Valley of Dry Bones
events.description: The Lord's hand led Ezekiel out in the Spirit and set him down in a valley full of dry bones. God asks: Can these bones become alive? Ezekiel answers: Lord God, you know it. God commands him to prophesy over the bones, and there is a rattling sound as bone joins to bone, sinews and flesh cover them, and skin draws over them. But there is no breath in them. Then Ezekiel prophesies to the breath, and the breath enters them so they stand up as an exceedingly great army. God explains that the bones are the whole house of Israel who say: Our bones are dry, our hope is lost. But God will open their graves, give them his Spirit, and bring them back to the land of Israel.

events.title: The Two Sticks – Israel Gathered
events.description: God commands Ezekiel to take two sticks and write on one: For Judah, and on the other: For Joseph (Ephraim). He is to hold them together in his hand so they become one. When the people ask what this means, Ezekiel is to answer that God will gather the Israelites from the nations and bring them back to their own land. They shall be one nation with one king, never again divided into two kingdoms. They will be cleansed from their sins, and God’s servant David shall be their king forever. God will make a covenant of peace with them and set his sanctuary among them forever.

events.title: Gog and Magog
events.description: God commands Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog in the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. In the last days God will bring Gog up against Israel’s land with a vast army from many nations, equipped with shields, swords, and armor. But when Gog attacks, God’s wrath will flare up. God will judge him with plague, blood, torrential rain, hail, fire, and sulfur. Gog’s army will fall on the mountains of Israel and become food for birds and wild animals. The cleanup work will take seven months, and the weapons will be burned for seven years. In this way all nations will know that the Lord is God.

events.title: The Vision of the New Temple
events.description: In the twenty-fifth year of the exile, on New Year's Day, God brings Ezekiel in a vision to the land of Israel and sets him on a high mountain. There he sees a man with an appearance like bronze holding a measuring cord and a measuring rod. The man measures out the entire new temple in detail: the gates, the courtyards, the temple hall, the Most Holy Place, and all the side rooms. Ezekiel is shown the temple from every side with precise measurements and proportions. The vision is a promise that God will restore his worship and dwell again among his people.

events.title: The Glory of the Lord Returns
events.description:
Ezekiel is brought to the east gate, and there he sees the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east.  
The sound is like the roar of great waters, and the earth shines with his glory.  
The vision is like what Ezekiel saw by the Kebar River and when the Lord's glory left the temple.  
The glory enters the temple through the east gate, and the Spirit lifts Ezekiel into the inner court.  
The Lord's glory fills the temple, and God speaks to Ezekiel from the temple: This is the place for my throne and the soles of my feet, where I will dwell among the Israelites forever.

events.title: The Water Flowing from the Temple
events.description: Ezekiel is brought back to the temple entrance and sees water flowing out from under the temple threshold toward the east. The man measures a thousand cubits, and the water reaches his ankles; another thousand cubits, and it reaches his knees; another thousand cubits, and it reaches his hips; and another thousand cubits, and it has become a river he cannot cross. Along the riverbank trees grow on both sides with leaves that never wither and fruit that never fails, for the water nourishing them flows from the sanctuary. The water flows down to the wilderness and out into the Dead Sea, and wherever the river reaches, life is restored.
